rewriteLast.title: Chapter 6 · Reddy Goes Hunting
rewriteLast.artPrompt: A moonlit meadow at the forest edge: a wise older fox and a young red fox freeze mid-prowl in the silver grass, one paw raised, both staring at a plump field mouse that nibbles seeds unaware, the moon high above and mist over the meadow. Silver-blue night tones with warm russet fur, hushed teaching mood, storybook illustration.

blocks.text: The moon was up over the Green Meadows, and Granny Fox said it was time. “Tonight, Reddy,” she said, “you will hunt your first real supper. Walk soft, keep downwind, and let your ears do the work while your feet stay quiet.”

They padded out into the silver grass. Reddy’s heart drummed with excitement. Somewhere under the moon a fat meadow mouse was nibbling seeds. He was sweet and plump, and perfectly unaware that two foxes were near. The mouse was lucky, for the moon kept his secret and the wind kept his smell.

Soon Reddy saw the grass quiver. He bunched his legs to spring — but Granny pressed him down gently with one paw. “Wait,” she whispered. “A wise fox waits until the mouse forgets the whole world. Then, and only then, he leaps.”
Granny holds Reddy back, one paw raised, until the mouse forgets to be afraid.
New word: downwind — hiding where your smell drifts away from the one you watch.

So Reddy waited, still as an old stump. The mouse nibbled. The mouse washed his whiskers. The mouse played a little game of pop-up on a tussock. He forgot the fox, and the moon, and the whole wide world. Then Granny nodded — and Reddy sprang. He trotted home through the damp grass with his first meadow mouse, and Granny’s eyes shone in the dark. “Well done, Reddy,” she said. “You waited, and so you ate. That is the oldest fox law there is.” It was the proudest walk of his whole young life.

“I am a hunter now,” Reddy told himself, walking proudly along the shadowy paths. And the thought sat warm in his chest all night long. Granny would have told him, if she had heard. A thought like that is a little too warm for a young fox’s safety.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Reddy Grows Careless
chapters.artPrompt: A proud young red fox struts along the top rail of a farm fence in broad afternoon sunshine, tail flaunting like a banner, while far off a farm boy by the red barn shades his eyes to look and a brown hound lifts his head from a doze. Golden hayfields and big summer clouds, bright but uneasy storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Reddy grew prouder every day. “I am the smartest fox in the Green Forest,” he told Jimmy Skunk. Jimmy was out strolling with his slow, polite smile. “I can outwait a mouse, outrun a hound, and outthink anybody.” Jimmy Skunk said nothing at all, which was very wise of him.

Granny Fox had one rule above all her rules: never hunt by daylight near the farm. But Reddy had begun to think rules were for younger foxes. One warm afternoon he trotted into the open and walked the pasture fence rail like a circus walker.

Far across the yard, Bowser the Hound lifted his head from his nap. And by the barn door, Farmer Brown’s boy shaded his eyes and looked, and looked again. “That,” he said slowly, “is a fox. In broad daylight.”
Reddy struts on the fence — while the boy watches and Bowser wakes.
Ask your child: Granny’s rule was never hunt by daylight near the farm. Why did Reddy think the rule was not for him?

Bowser came across the yard like a brown thunderbolt, baying at every jump. Reddy leaped from the fence and ran, and this time it was not a game. The hound was close — too close — and Reddy had to use every trick Granny had ever taught him. He ran the stone wall where his feet left no smell. He doubled through the brambles. He slipped along the ditch and at last left Bowser howling at an empty hole in the ground. Reddy did not stop to laugh this time. He did not stop for anything.

That evening Granny Fox looked at him a long, long time. “The boy has seen you now, Reddy,” she said quietly. “Men with eyes remember.” Reddy shrugged and boastfully washed his whiskers. But all night, somewhere far off, he could hear Bowser still talking to the moon.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Raid on the Henhouse
chapters.artPrompt: A dark moonless night at the red henhouse: a young red fox slips out of the low doorway with a white hen in his jaws, loose feathers drifting, while a lantern swings from the farmhouse porch and a door bangs open far behind. Deep blue-black night with one slice of warm light, exciting storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Reddy had walked away from the henhouse once, on a bright night, counting to ten. But he had told everyone how brave he was, and showing off is a hungry habit. Each night the warm hen smell drifted across the fields, and each night it grew harder to say no.

“One little hen,” said the hungry voice inside him. “Granny will never know.” Granny always knew. But pride plugged Reddy’s ears, and hunger shut his eyes. At last, on a moonless night, he crept across the fields to Farmer Brown’s yard.

The henhouse door was shut but not fastened. Reddy nosed it, and it swung. Inside, the hens slept in a warm row, murmuring in their dreams. Reddy’s mouth watered until his whiskers curled. His paws were quick, but his breath came faster, and his grin had gone quite stiff.
Reddy slips from the henhouse with a hen — and the farm wakes up.

He caught a plump white hen, and the henhouse exploded into squawks. A dog barked. A window banged up. A lantern swung out onto the porch, and a voice shouted across the yard. Reddy ran for the fields with the hen over his shoulder and his heart in his mouth. He reached the Green Forest, breathing hard, and ate his stolen supper under the black pines. And it tasted, he could not help noticing, not quite as sweet as usual. A meadow mouse caught honestly on a moonlit hunt always tasted better.
New word: fastened — shut tight, so it cannot swing open by itself.

Far away the farm lights burned late. Granny Fox found him there and sat down without a word. “Now they know your face, Reddy,” she said at last. “And tomorrow, they will be looking for it.” Reddy said nothing at all, and for once, that was the smartest thing he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Gun in the Cornfield
chapters.artPrompt: A young red fox races along a row of a dawn-lit cornfield, ears flat and body low, a puff of dust kicking up from the stubble behind him where a shot has just missed, while far back at the fence a farm boy holds a gun and a baying hound strains on the lead. Pale gold morning light, swift and dramatic but softened, storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Farmer Brown’s boy did not forget. All the next day he walked the fields with his gun, while Bowser sniffed every fence corner. And the morning after, just as the sun came up, Bowser found a fresh trail. It led straight to Reddy’s cover.

Reddy ran. He ran the old paths at the top of his speed. Behind him, Bowser’s great voice boomed like a drum. He was halfway down the cornfield when he heard a sound he had never heard before. Reddy’s legs were strong, but a hound’s legs are strong too, and a hound does not give up.
“Bang!” A white puff of smoke jumped from the fence corner. Something hot stung across Reddy’s shoulder, like a giant wasp. He tumbled, rolled, and was up and running before the dust had settled.
Reddy runs the cornfield as the shot kicks up the dust behind him.
New word: grazed — touched lightly as it passed by, the way the shot touched Reddy.

It was only a graze, a hot stripe across his fur. But it frightened Reddy more than any hound ever had. He left the cornfield in one long leap and slipped into the deep brambles. No hound and no gun could come there. He did not stop until the Green Forest closed behind him like a door. All that day he lay hidden, licking his shoulder, listening to Bowser’s voice grow tired and far away. He was thirsty, and sore, and very small-feeling. For the first time in his whole proud life, Reddy Fox wanted his Granny. That evening he heard the boy calling Bowser home, and the two went back to the farm without him.
When full dark came, a soft footstep came down the bramble path. Granny Fox set down a fresh-caught mouse beside him, and said, gently, “Eat, Reddy. Then we will go home.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Granny Keeps Watch
chapters.artPrompt: Inside a dim earth den lit by one thin shaft of daylight: a young red fox lies curled on dry leaves with his shoulder packed in soft moss, while a wise older fox gently licks his ear and a fresh-caught mouse waits on a leaf beside him, rain dripping at the entrance. Warm amber den glow against cool grey light, tender storybook illustration.

blocks.text: The den under the old stump was dark and quiet and smelled of home. Reddy lay on the dry leaves, holding his sore shoulder still. Granny Fox washed it gently, the way she had washed him when he was small.

“Does it still sting?” she asked. “Only when I forget and stretch,” said Reddy. “Then do not forget,” said Granny. And there was so much love under her gruffness that Reddy had to look away and pretend his ear itched. A wound inside a den needs two things: rest, and somebody to wait on you.

Every night she hunted for two, and every morning she brought him the pick of the catch. The days went by, and the stripe on his shoulder healed to a thin pale line. Granny counted the days on her toes, and never once hurried him.
Granny brings Reddy the pick of the catch, night after night.
Ask your child: Granny scolded Reddy, but she also hunted for him every night. What does that show about love?

“Now, Reddy,” she said one evening, “we will talk. You paid for one stolen hen with a hot stripe, with Bowser’s teeth, and with the boy’s gun. Was it worth it?” And Reddy, looking at his pale stripe, said, “No, Granny. It was not.”

“A wise fox keeps his wits sharper than his appetite,” said Granny Fox. “Say it back to me.” And Reddy said it back, twice, so that it would stay in him through all the hungry nights to come. He slept that night the sleep of a fox with nothing on his mind. Outside, the rain whispered on the stump, and the Green Forest stood guard. Granny curled round him like a warm red question mark. And somewhere far off, the farm slept too, and nobody dreamed of foxes at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Smoke at the Den Door
chapters.artPrompt: A farm boy crouches at a den entrance under old tree roots, feeding a small smoking fire of damp leaves while a brown hound whines beside him; on the far hill in plain view a wise old fox sits looking back over her shoulder, morning mist on the meadow. Cool grey-blue light with one small orange fire glow, suspenseful but safe storybook illustration.

blocks.text: But the boy did not give up. He had watched the brambles, and the ditches, and at last he found the old stump. Beneath it was the den, with the fresh fox smell at the door.

He came with Bowser on the lead and an armful of dry leaves. “We will smoke him out,” he said, and he knelt and struck a match. Soon a thin grey smoke crept down into the den, curling like a ghost. The smoke did not smell like supper, or like danger. It only smelled like a very bad idea.
Reddy coughed. But he was not afraid, and this is why: the den had a second door. Long ago, Granny Fox had dug a back way out, under the brambles, for just such a morning as this.
Granny shows herself on the far hill, and the boy forgets the smoke.
New word: curling — moving in soft round shapes, like smoke or sleeping cats.

Then Granny Fox walked out onto the far hill, in full view, calm as Sunday. She sat down. She looked back over her shoulder. And the boy forgot all about his match and his smoke. “The old fox!” he cried, and off he ran, with Bowser pulling and straining at the lead. Granny led them a merry dance — along the fence, across the ditch, around the great field, over the stile. By the end of it, boy and hound were tired and far from home. Then she whisked into the tall corn, and the meadow was empty. Not one paw print, not one red hair, told them where she had gone.
By the time the boy came back to the stump, the smoke was thin and grey. And the den was empty too. Reddy was safe in the deep woods. That very night he and Granny laughed about it over supper.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Reddy’s Promise
chapters.artPrompt: A young red fox sits at the mouth of his den at sunset, a thin pale scar on his healed shoulder, gazing toward faraway farm lights, while a wise older fox sits close beside him and a striped skunk passes politely on the path below. Rosy evening light, calm and settled mood, storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Reddy’s shoulder healed, and the pale stripe faded into his red coat. But the lesson did not fade. Every time he smelled hens on the wind, his shoulder remembered the sting of the gun. And his feet turned the other way.

“No more henhouses,” he told Granny Fox, out loud, at the mouth of the den. “I keep to mice and moles and the meadow’s own bounty. A wise fox keeps his wits sharper than his appetite.” And he said it again on the second evening, in case the first time had not carried.
Granny said nothing at all, but she smiled her quiet smile. And Jimmy Skunk, passing below on his evening stroll, nodded once. It was as much as to say that the Green Forest had noticed.
Reddy makes his promise at the den door, with Granny beside him.
Ask your child: Reddy’s promise was hard to keep. What helped him keep it?

It was not always easy. On cold nights the farm smell came across the fields, warm and easy and wrong. On those nights Reddy made himself remember the white puff of smoke and the sting. Then he went hunting in the meadow instead. And every morning the meadow paid him back in mice and peace of mind. And here is the strange thing: the meadow fed him well. His coat grew glossier, his eyes brighter, and he never once had to run from a lantern again. Honest suppers, it turns out, come with quiet dreams. Jimmy Skunk told Peter Rabbit, and Peter Rabbit told Johnny Chuck, and soon the whole Green Meadows knew.
Season by season, the little people of the Green Forest began to say a new thing about Reddy Fox. They said it quietly, and they said it truly: “Reddy is smart. Reddy is smart now.”

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Smartest Fox in the Forest
chapters.artPrompt: Autumn in the Green Forest at golden hour: a grown, self-possessed red fox sits on a mossy knoll beside his wise old grandmother, both gazing over the valley as maple leaves drift down and the farm becomes a tiny warm dot far below. Rich reds, russets and deep greens, mellow slanting light, proud peaceful storybook finale illustration.

blocks.text: Seasons went by, and Reddy grew big and strong, with a deep red coat and a fine white-tipped brush. He no longer showed off on fences. He listened more than he talked, and his nose stayed busy, just as Granny had taught him. The farm lights below were only little golden stars, and he no longer counted them as supper.
He taught the young foxes what Granny had taught him: walk soft, keep downwind, wait until the world forgets you. And when they asked about the pale stripe on his shoulder, he told them the truth.

“I stole a hen once,” he said, “and it cost me more than the hen was worth. Take it from Reddy Fox: the meadow feeds an honest fox better than any farm ever will.” The young foxes believed him at once, for truth has a ring that boasting never has.
Reddy and Granny watch the autumn valley, side by side.
Ask your child: what made Reddy truly smart — his tricks, or his lessons?
The little people of the Green Forest said, “Reddy Fox is clever.” And Granny Fox said nothing at all. She only smiled her quiet smile — the one she saved for things that had turned out right.

One golden evening they sat together on the mossy knoll, watching the leaves drift down. Far below, the farm lights twinkled, warm and small and safe. “Granny,” said Reddy, “you were right about everything.” “I know,” said Granny. And the wind stirred the maples, and the valley turned amber, and the smartest fox in the forest sat content. For he had learned the best trick of all: knowing when not to use one. The leaves came down like gold rain, and neither fox moved for a long, happy while.
